about.sources: Church Latin, tier 3, is six short readings. They are not beginner Latin. Augustine is the public-domain text of the Confessiones in Migne’s 1841 edition: book 1, chapter 1, from Magnus es, Domine through the second aliqua portiō creātūrae tuae, then the next sentence, and book 10, chapter 27, from Sērō tē amāvī through tēcum nōn eram. The parenthetical verse numbers in that edition are the editor’s, so they are not part of these sentences. Thomas Aquinas is the Leonine text (Rome, 1888) of the Summa theologiae: the prologue through ad ērudītiōnem incipientium, First Part, question 1, article 8, reply to the second objection, and the opening sentence of the reply in article 1. The English is a new literal translation made for this app. Macrons follow this app’s spelling; the Leonine tanquam is shown as tamquam. The words themselves are not rewritten, and no biblical sentence has been added.

words.en: to serve under, be subject to
1, in a biblical citation (not the verb eō)
Corinthians, abbreviated Corinth. in a citation

lines.en: Great are you, Lord, and greatly to be praised: great is your power, and of your wisdom there is no number.

And a human being, some portion of your creation, wants to praise you; and a human being carrying around his mortality, carrying around the testimony of his sin and the testimony that you resist the proud; and still a human being, some portion of your creation, wants to praise you.
You stir us, so that praising you delights us, because you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you!
And see: you were inside, and I was outside, and there I was looking for you; and upon those beautiful things which you made, I, misshapen, was rushing.
You were with me, and I was not with you.
Because a teacher of Catholic truth ought not only to instruct those who are advanced, but it also belongs to him to teach beginners,
according to that saying of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 3, “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk as a drink, not solid food,”
the purpose of our intention in this work is to hand on the things that belong to the Christian religion in the way that suits the instruction of beginners.
For since grace does not take away nature, but perfects it, natural reason should serve faith, just as the natural inclination of the will complies with charity.

texts.title: Summa I, q. 1, a. 1, the reply

lines.en: I answer that it must be said that, for human salvation, there needed to be some teaching according to divine revelation, besides the philosophical disciplines, which are investigated by human reason.

lessons.title: Confessions: praise and frailty
lessons.sum: Harder reading. Magnus es, Domine, through the second aliqua portiō.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Augustine’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Magnus es and laudābilis describe tū, which the verb es already names. Magna virtūs tua and sapientiae tuae nōn est numerus are two more statements: “great is your power,” and “of your wisdom there is no number.” Sapientiae tuae is genitive.

Laudāre is the infinitive, the object of vult. Homō is “a human being.” Aliqua portiō creātūrae tuae is in apposition with it: “some portion of your creation.” Circumferēns is a present participle agreeing with homō, “carrying around.” Peccātī suī is genitive, “of his own sin.” Superbīs is dative plural, “the proud,” with resistis.
lessons.diff: Migne prints verse numbers in parentheses after valdē, numerus, and resistis. Those notes are the editor’s. They are not part of this sentence. The passage stops at the second aliqua portiō creātūrae tuae.

qs: there is no number of the proud

lessons.title: Confessions: our heart is restless
lessons.sum: Harder reading. The next sentence, Tū excitās.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Augustine’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
This is the next sentence of the same chapter, not a new paragraph of Augustine’s. Excitās is second person: “you stir (us) up.” The ut clause takes the subjunctive dēlectet. Its subject is the infinitive laudāre tē: “so that praising you delights.”

Fēcistī nōs ad tē is “you made us toward yourself,” the ordinary way of saying “for yourself.” Inquiētum est cor nostrum “our heart is restless.” Dōnec requiēscat is “until it rests,” with the subjunctive of requiēscō. In tē is “in you.”

lessons.title: Confessions: late have I loved you
lessons.sum: Harder reading. Sērō tē amāvī through tēcum nōn eram.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Augustine’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Sērō is the adverb “late,” not a verb. Pulchritūdō is vocative, addressed as “beauty.” Tam antīqua et tam nova agrees with it. The second sērō tē amāvī repeats the first.

Intus erās “you were inside.” Ego forīs “I was outside.” Forīs is the adverb, not a form of forum. Ibī tē quaerēbam “there I kept looking for you.” In ista fōrmōsa “upon those beautiful things,” with quae fēcistī “which you made.” Dēformis describes ego. Mēcum and tēcum are “with me” and “with you.”
lessons.diff: The chapter continues Ea mē tenēbant longē ā tē. That sentence is not part of this lesson. The reading ends at tēcum nōn eram.

lessons.title: Summa: why this book
lessons.sum: Harder reading. One sentence, Quia Catholicae vēritātis doctor.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Aquinas’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
This is one sentence, printed here in three lines so it can be read. Quia gives the reason. Doctor is the subject. Catholicae vēritātis is genitive, “of Catholic truth.” Nōn sōlum prōvectōs “not only the advanced”: prōvectōs is the participle of prōvehō. Dēbet īnstruere “ought to instruct.” Then ad eum pertinet “it belongs to him,” with ērudīre “to teach.”

Secundum illud apostolī “according to that saying of the Apostle.” Apostolī is genitive singular. I ad Corinth. III is the Leonine citation “1 Corinthians 3,” not the verb eō and not the number trēs. Tamquam parvulīs “as to little children,” dative. Lac vōbīs pōtum dedī “I gave you milk as a drink.” The Leonine prints tanquam; this app shows tamquam.

The main clause is prōpositum nostrae intentiōnis est trādere “the purpose of our intention is to hand on.” Ea quae ad Chrīstiānam religiōnem pertinent is the object. Eō modō “in that way,” both ablative. Incipientium is genitive plural of the participle, “of beginners.”
lessons.diff: The words I ad Corinth. III and the milk sentence are inside Aquinas’s sentence in the Leonine edition. They are not an extra passage added here. The sentence ends at ad ērudītiōnem incipientium.

lessons.title: Summa: grace and nature
lessons.sum: Harder reading. Cum enim grātia nōn tollat nātūram.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Aquinas’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Cum here means “since,” with the subjunctive tollat and perficiat. Grātia is the subject of both. Nātūram is the object: grace does not take nature away, but perfects it.

Oportet quod “it is necessary that,” with subserviat subjunctive. Nātūrālis ratiō is the subject, “natural reason.” Fideī is dative, “faith.” The comparison is sīcut et “just as also.” Inclīnātiō voluntātis “the inclination of the will,” genitive. Obsequitur cāritātī “complies with charity,” and cāritātī is dative.
lessons.aside: This sentence, not the short saying
lessons.diff: The sentence in the Leonine reply is the whole of what is printed here, including enim and sīcut et nātūrālis inclīnātiō voluntātis obsequitur cāritātī. A shorter proverb that drops those words is not this text.

lessons.title: Summa: why revelation
lessons.sum: Harder reading. The opening Respondeō of question 1, article 1.
lessons.lead: This is not beginner Latin. The Latin is Aquinas’s own sentence, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Respondeō dīcendum quod is the ordinary opening of a reply: “I answer that it must be said that.” Dīcendum is the neuter gerundive of dīcō. Necessārium fuit “it was necessary,” with the infinitive esse: “that there be.”

Ad hūmānam salūtem “for human salvation.” Doctrīnam quandam secundum revēlātiōnem dīvīnam “some teaching according to divine revelation.” Praeter philosophicās disciplīnās “besides the philosophical disciplines,” accusative after praeter. Quae ratiōne hūmānā investīgantur “which are investigated by human reason.” Ratiōne hūmānā is ablative.
lessons.diff: The reply continues with Prīmō quidem. That next sentence is not in this lesson. Nothing here is a commentary on the Hail Mary.
